No exact witness value can be constructed for any positive claim because the fragment derives no concrete sector_num/nb_sectors magnitudes and the line 9 gate's admitted set is not shown.

verdict.summary: snprintf's size argument is computed from the attacker-controlled username length (18 + userName_size + 1) instead of the actual buffer capacity; buffer_size is passed at the call site but never used. With a username of 12 or more characters, the 30-byte stack buffer declared in main is written past its end (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: The size argument 18 + userName_size + 1 = 19 + n is derived from userName_size, whose residual range is any n >= 0 (provenance: strlen(argv[1]) at line 29, unconstrained by any shown check; the argc guard at line 22 admits all lengths). The declared destination capacity is 30 bytes (char buffer[30]; line 28) and the intended bound buffer_size (= sizeof(buffer) = 30) is passed at line 29 but never used in the body. For any n >= 12, 19 + n > 30, so snprintf writes 18 + n content characters plus the NUL into a 30-byte object, overrunning by n - 11 bytes (e.g., n = 12 writes 31 bytes). This is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) caused by a missing bound: the input-derived size is never compared or clamped against the visible 30-byte capacity.

assumptions: Destination capacity is exactly 30 bytes: declared at line 28 (char buffer[30];) and passed as buffer_size = sizeof(buffer) at line 29.
snprintf's standard semantics: writes at most size-1 characters plus a terminating NUL, and returns the would-be length (return value discarded at line 16).
The required output length is derived from the literal format string visible at line 16: 17-byte prefix, n-byte username, 1-byte suffix, plus NUL.
limitations: The witness uses n = 12, a boundary value computed entirely from shown constants (18 + 1 in the size expression and 30 in the declaration); the underlying claim is a range claim over all n >= 12, which is fully admitted since no shown statement constrains the username length.
The discarded snprintf return value (line 16) is not independently security-relevant; the defect is the oversized write itself.
printf("%s", buffer) at line 30 is safe: it uses a literal format string with buffer as an argument, so no format-string finding.

verdict.summary: The int parameter nal_length_size reaches the loop counter with no positivity/lower-bound check. The guard at line 4 (`if (end - start < nal_length_size)`) is false for every negative nal_length_size when the buffer is non-empty, so `while (nal_length_size--)` starts at a negative value and decrements forever (pre-decrement values -1, -2, ... are always truthy and never reach 0). The loop never terminates (CWE-835), and each iteration executes `*start++` at line 7, continuing past `end` into out-of-bounds memory (OOB read) until the process faults; the line-8 checks are unreachable because the loop never exits. No shown statement bounds nal_length_size to a positive width.

evidence.reason: nal_length_size is a signed int parameter whose residual range is unconstrained: the only guard, line 4 (`if (end - start < nal_length_size)`), rejects a value only when fewer than that many bytes remain, so with a valid non-empty buffer every negative value is admitted (e.g., end - start = 8, nal_length_size = -1: 8 < -1 is false). The loop condition tests the pre-decrement value, so a negative start value yields -1, -2, -3, ... which are all truthy and never become 0, so the loop never terminates (CWE-835) and the read `*start++` at line 7 executes without bound, dereferencing past `end` (out-of-bounds read consequence) once the buffer is exhausted. The protective checks at line 8 are unreachable on this path because control never exits the loop, and no shown statement requires nal_length_size >= 1.

assumptions: start and end are treated as delimiting a readable buffer [start, end) per the function's contract; the fragment itself never verifies start != NULL or start <= end.
int is 32-bit two's complement (standard for the shown types; the negative-counter witness does not depend on it).
limitations: start is dereferenced at line 7 with no NULL check, so a NULL start passed with nal_length_size >= 1 would be a NULL dereference (CWE-476); treated as a contractual robustness concern secondary to the loop finding and not reported as an independent CWE.

For nal_length_size >= 4, `(res << 8)` at line 7 overflows signed int (UB); a negative res from a 4-byte 0xFF length is rejected by `res < 0` at line 8, and no concrete out-of-domain consumption of an overflowed value was demonstrated — recorded as a robustness/UB concern only.

The line-8 operand `start + res > end` evaluates pointer arithmetic before the `res < 0` short-circuit when res is negative; the practical outcome is still return NULL, so no exploitable failure was demonstrated.
An end < start window combined with a sufficiently negative nal_length_size also passes line 4 and hit the same non-terminating loop; folded into the same finding.

The 4-byte negative-length rejection (`res < 0`) and the pointer-wrap check (`start + res < start`) correctly neutralize the positive-width length-field hazards; the remaining defect is exclusively the missing lower bound on nal_length_size.

verdict.summary: In on_resolver_result_changed_locked, the resolver-provided GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES argument is extracted at line 28 (channel_arg->value.pointer.p into grpc_lb_addresses *addresses) and immediately dereferenced at line 30 in the loop condition (addresses->num_addresses). The only preceding guards are the arg-presence check (line 26) and the type-tag assert (line 27), neither of which constrains the pointer value; a NULL value.pointer.p therefore passes every guard and causes a NULL-pointer crash (DoS) in the resolution path.

evidence.reason: Sink dereferences `addresses`, which was assigned from the unconditionally unchecked payload field `channel_arg->value.pointer.p` (line 28). `value.pointer.p` is entry-point resolver data whose residual range is the full pointer domain including NULL: line 26 only checks that the arg entry exists, and line 27 (GPR_ASSERT(type == GRPC_ARG_POINTER)) only checks the type tag, so a NULL pointer passes both guards in order (13 -> 26 -> 27 -> 28 -> 30) and is dereferenced at line 30 (`addresses->num_addresses`) and again at line 31 (`addresses->addresses[i]`). No statement between extraction and use tests or derives a non-NULL value, so the absence of the NULL check is the confirmed CWE-476 mechanism; impact is a client-process crash on attacker-influenced or malformed resolver data.

assumptions: `chand->resolver_result` and its contained `grpc_arg` entries are resolver-callback payloads derived from external resolution data; the fragment's only constraint is the non-NULL check on the container at line 13.
`channel_arg->value.pointer.p` is read as a pointer-typed value whose full declared domain (including NULL) is admitted by the shown checks at lines 26-27.
limitations: Reachable-abort candidates CWE-617 at GPR_ASSERT lines 18, 27, and 66: a resolver payload carrying a mismatched type tag aborts the process, but the trigger depends on internal struct-consistency of the payload, so this is kept as a lower-confidence concern, not a verdict CWE.

Log-injection candidate CWE-117 at gpr_log lines 38-42: the resolver-supplied LB policy name is written via a fixed %s format with no CR/LF sanitization; confirmed only as a low-impact, lower-confidence concern and excluded from the verdict.

OOB-read candidate over `addresses->addresses[i]` (line 31): the index is bounded by the payload's own `num_addresses` and the backing array capacity is not visible in the fragment, so an excess cannot be demonstrated from shown arithmetic; treated as a missing-capacity/hardening concern.

`gpr_strdup` at line 67 may return NULL on allocation failure and is passed to `grpc_service_config_create` at line 69; this is an unchecked environment-allocation path, not attacker-directed, so it is not a finding.
Single-shot cleanup ordering (strdup at line 80 before destroy at line 81; old-lb-policy unref guarded at line 149) is correct and not a finding.

verdict.summary: The JNI wrapper forwards the caller-supplied cpIndex (signed jint, full domain -2^31..2^31-1) unchanged to the indexed constant-pool accessor getFieldAt at line 4 with no bounds or sign validation in the shown code; a negative or oversized index triggers an out-of-bounds read of the constant pool (missing bound / unvalidated index flow), CWE-125.

evidence.snippet: return getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);
evidence.reason: Sink is the indexed accessor getFieldAt, whose third argument cpIndex is, by callee and parameter name, a constant-pool index. cpIndex retains its full signed jint residual range because the fragment contains no constraint between the parameter declaration (line 2) and this call; there are no guards, so e.g. cpIndex = -1 is admitted and reaches the sink, an out-of-domain value for any indexed access, and no pool capacity is declared anywhere in the shown code (missing bound / unvalidated index flow). This yields an out-of-bounds read of constant-pool memory (CWE-125).

assumptions: jint is the JNI-specified signed 32-bit integer type, domain [-2^31, 2^31-1].
getFieldAt is an indexed accessor into the constant pool as implied by its name and by the argument name cpIndex.
The flags J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME and J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL are callee arguments, not constraints on cpIndex in the shown code.
limitations: The getFieldAt callee body is not shown, so the exact read extent, whether the access can be a write, and any internal signed-to-unsigned conversion (CWE-195) cannot be demonstrated; the finding anchors on the call-site index argument being out of domain.
constantPoolOop is forwarded without a NULL check, but the shown code performs no dereference, so no NULL-dereference finding is reported.
The returned jobject is not inspected, but the function's contract is to propagate the result, so this is not reported as an error-handling flaw.

verdict.summary: Not vulnerable. The certificate-name allowlist pairing is protected by the boundary guard at line 20, which admits only an exact-length match (len >= strlen(signature_name), equivalent to equality given the prefix match) or a match whose first byte after the trusted prefix is whitespace (isspace(signature_name[len])). Every prefix match with a non-whitespace continuation falls through the loop and is routed to the user prompt and TRUST_E_EXPLICIT_DISTRUST at lines 24-28, so no silent-trust bypass is reachable from the shown statements. All function returns (GetSignatureName, utf8_to_wchar, WinVerifyTrust, MessageBoxExU) are checked or consumed correctly; no memory-safety, injection, or logic flaw is confirmed.

assumptions: signature_name (L11) is treated as a NUL-terminated C string by the shown code: it is consumed by strncmp/strlen (L18-L19), indexed at signature_name[len] (L20), and formatted with '%s' (L25), so the NUL-terminated-string contract is the visible invariant.

cert_name is a global array of NUL-terminated strings whose element count is ARRAYSIZE(cert_name); accesses cert_name[i] are in-bounds for i in [0, ARRAYSIZE-1] solely by the loop condition at line 17.
GetSignatureName may derive signature_name from content inside the file at path; even under the full residual range (any non-NULL NUL-terminated string) the conclusion of Phase 4 holds.
trust_file.pcwszFilePath is freed (L52) only after WinVerifyTrust (L51) consumes it; no use-after-free is visible.
limitations: isspace(signature_name[len]) at line 20 passes a possibly-signed char; a continuation byte >= 0x80 with signed char is undefined behavior per the C ctype contract. The outcome on admitted inputs cannot be determined from the shown statements, and under the strongest protective reading it rejects (routes to lines 24-28), so no bypass is demonstrable; treated as a portability/robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

The guard at line 20 deliberately admits exact matches and whitespace-continuation matches of a trusted cert_name entry. Whether an adversary can obtain a certificate whose subject falls into that admitted set depends on the unshown contents of cert_name and external CA issuance, which the fragment cannot establish; any such claim fails Phase 3 part 2 reachability.

signature_name and path are passed un-sanitized to log/UI sinks (uprintf at lines 25, 34; lmprintf at line 26). A CR/LF-bearing signature subject could reach line 25, but an unambiguous witness must avoid every cert_name entry whose contents are unshown, and the local log has no structured backend visible; demoted, no CWE.

No free of signature_name is shown (potential single-shot leak) and the internals of GetSignatureName, utf8_to_wchar, uprintf, and lmprintf are not shown; allocation failure of utf8_to_wchar is NULL-checked (L33), and the environment-failure path is not attacker-directed at scale, so it is not a finding.
The ultimate consumer of the returned r (L67) is not shown; the trust decision's final use is outside the fragment.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only input-derived memory operation is the comment-append path (lines 116-120): the allocation strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2 exactly bounds the written bytes comment + ' ' + nc + NUL, since the in-place unescape/ANSI-strip transforms (lines 113-114) are length-non-increasing by standard semantics (worst case no escapes gives an exact fit; escaped input shrinks). Every other input flow is NULL-gated (lines 17, 28, 31, 44, 61, 95, 161, 169, 171, 210), uses constant format strings (lines 19, 23, 33, 98, 129-130), or consumes framework-provided data (loop bound bb->size at line 66). OOM-dependent and unshown-callee concerns are recorded in limitations, not as findings.

assumptions: input is the NUL-terminated 'CC'-prefixed command string, so the input[1]/input[2]/input[3] reads at lines 3, 11, 13, 53, 146, 195 are in-bounds and input+2/input+3 pointers formed at lines 8, 75, 89, 109, 147, 157 are within the string or at the NUL terminator.
r_meta_set_string/r_meta_set deep-copy their string arguments; the shown code frees the buffers immediately after the calls (lines 21, 25, 102, 122, 137, 174, 214).

r_str_unescape and r_str_ansi_strip are in-place, length-non-increasing transforms, which is what makes the line 116 allocation (strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2) exactly cover the writes at lines 118-120.
bb->size and fcn->bbs at lines 64-70 are framework-provided analysis data, not derived from the command input in the shown code.
limitations: The non-expansion of the transforms at lines 113-114 is implied by their names/standard semantics but not proven inside the fragment; if a transform could expand the string, the line 116 allocation could be undersized for line 120.

NULL-use of r_str_newf/strdup/r_core_undo_new results (lines 20, 24, 112-114, 127, 129-132, 167, 183, 212-213) requires allocator failure on ordinary string sizes; treated as environmental robustness, not confirmed.
A 1-byte OOB read of input[1] at line 3 would require an empty command string, which depends on an unshown dispatcher guarantee for the CC handler.

Line 130 builds an undo command string b embedding the raw comment nc; whether the unshown undo machinery later executes b as a command (potential command injection) cannot be confirmed from this fragment.
r_core_editor is called with a possibly-NULL comment at line 94; its NULL behavior is unshown.

verdict.summary: Java_sun_reflect_ConstantPool_getFieldAtIfLoaded0 forwards the JNI parameter cpIndex (jint, full signed 32-bit domain) with no bounds check into getFieldAt() as a constant-pool index. A Java caller can pass a negative value such as -1, or any value beyond the pool size, reaching the sink at line 4 and driving an out-of-bounds constant-pool access (missing validation of an input-derived index).

evidence.reason: cpIndex is an entry-point JNI parameter (jint) with full residual range [-2^31, 2^31-1]: the fragment (lines 1-4) imposes no comparison, cast, length cap, or pool-size bound on it. It flows unchanged to this sink as the index argument of getFieldAt, which consumes it as a constant-pool index. No visible capacity for the constant pool exists in the fragment, so the shown code derives an out-of-domain index: cpIndex = -1 (and any value above the real pool size, e.g., 0x7FFFFFFF) is a member of the residual range, passes the zero guards on the path, and reaches line 4 on the single straight-line path, causing out-of-bounds constant-pool read (CWE-125); the missing bound itself is the confirmed defect.

assumptions: cpIndex is externally supplied across the JNI boundary from Java reflection code (entry-point input).
getFieldAt consumes its third argument as a constant-pool index, per the function name and the call-site usage; no capacity or bound for the constant pool is visible in the fragment.
Every execution path is the single straight-line sequence: declaration (line 2) to the return call (line 4).
limitations: No constant-pool capacity is shown, so the exact excess of the out-of-bounds access cannot be computed; per the OOB standard this is a confirmed missing-bound (unvalidated-index) flow rather than a computed-excess claim.
Callee-internal semantics of getFieldAt (read vs. write, and any jint-to-unsigned conversion) are not visible; a secondary CWE-195 or CWE-787 is plausible but not independently confirmed.
A NULL dereference of constantPoolOop cannot be confirmed because no dereference of it occurs in the shown code.
The unchecked NULL-return propagation from getFieldAt is standard JNI error signaling; no security-relevant operation runs on a failure state in the shown code, so it is not a finding.
No branches or loops exist in the fragment, so Branch/Loop walk and termination analysis are vacuous.

verdict.summary: Path traversal (tar-slip): the path-safety gate is a stub — is_path_safe() at line 172 unconditionally returns true — so archive entry names containing '../' (line 115/138) pass the first-pass check at line 116 unconstrained, are joined to dest_path at line 140 with the traversal intact, and are written outside the extraction root by archive_write_header (line 144) and archive_write_data_block (line 157). The disk writer is configured with only ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME|ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM (lines 78, 103), so no built-in libarchive dot-dot/symlink protection applies.

evidence.reason: CWE-22 path traversal confirmed at the file-creation sink. current_file (from archive_entry_pathname(entry), line 138) is attacker-controlled archive data whose residual range is every string: the only content guard, line 116 'if (!is_path_safe(current_file))', admits all values because is_path_safe returns true unconditionally at line 172, and no ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT/ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS option is set (flags at line 78, applied at line 103). A witness entry named '../../tmp/owned' with dest_path='/srv/uploads' passes line 82 (non-NULL), line 116 (guard returns true), and reaches full_path computed at line 140 '/srv/uploads/../../tmp/owned' (traversal preserved), is stored via archive_entry_set_pathname (line 142), and this call creates the file outside the destination root. Guard insufficiency: the check's admitted set is the full string domain, so the danger is not excluded.

CWE-22 data-write sink for the same traversal. The entry pathname was replaced at line 142 with the traversal-containing full_path computed at line 140 from dest_path and the unconstrained current_file (line 138), which passed the stub guard at line 116 (is_path_safe always true, line 172). This call writes the archive entry's data to the escaped path (e.g., dest_path/'../../tmp/owned'), completing arbitrary file write outside the extraction directory.

assumptions: archive_entry_pathname() return values and archive_read_* statuses follow their standard libarchive semantics; the fragment itself imposes no constraint on entry name content.
full_path capacity is the declared char full_path[PATH_MAX] (line 139) with PATH_MAX 512 (line 11); snprintf at line 140 enforces the cap, so no buffer overflow occurs there.
The sink calls (archive_write_header, archive_write_data_block) consume the entry pathname exactly as derived by the shown code (lines 140-142).
limitations: Symlink-based escape (CWE-59) is possible with the same root cause — no path vetting and no ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS — but is not reported as a separate CWE because it shares the identical missing-control mechanism.
snprintf truncation at line 140 for concatenations over 511 bytes can silently alter the extraction target; it is a robustness/logic concern, not a memory-safety defect.
Re-opening tar_path between passes (lines 125-130) creates a TOCTOU window if the archive is swapped, but the race is not demonstrated within the fragment, so it is not a confirmed finding.

The first-pass loop's exit status (line 114) is discarded and the second pass ignores archive_read_data_block errors at line 156; both are error-handling weaknesses, subsumed by the stub check but otherwise producer-dependent.
Passing a hypothetical NULL current_file to %s at line 140 is not confirmed because the fragment shows no path that produces NULL from archive_entry_pathname.

verdict.summary: avc_mp4_find_startcode reads out of bounds when nal_length_size is negative: the only pre-loop guard (line 4, `if (end - start < nal_length_size)`) admits every value <= end - start, including all negative ints, so `while (nal_length_size--)` (line 6) with e.g. nal_length_size == -1 never reaches 0 and `*start++` (line 7) reads ~2^32 bytes, far past `end`. A non-negativity/length validation is missing; the post-loop NULL check (line 8) runs after the reads and cannot protect them.

evidence.reason: nal_length_size is an int parameter whose full declared domain includes negative values; the only pre-loop guard (line 4, `if (end - start < nal_length_size) return NULL;`) admits every value <= end - start, and for a valid buffer (end - start >= 0) that set includes ALL negative ints. Witness: nal_length_size = -1 with end - start = 1: line 4 (`1 < -1`) is false, so the loop at line 6 runs while the counter is nonzero; a purely decrementing negative counter never reaches 0 (only wraparound through INT_MIN, UB, eventually returns via positives), so `*start++` at line 7 reads one byte per iteration and passes `end` at iteration end - start + 1 — an unbounded out-of-bounds read. The post-loop bound at line 8 (`if (res > end - start)`) executes after the reads and cannot protect them; the missing protective statement is validation that nal_length_size is positive and within bounds. CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read).

assumptions: start/end denote a valid [start, end) buffer so that end - start >= 0 and the pointer subtraction at line 4 is defined; the shown guards themselves rely on this.
unsigned int is 32-bit and the comparisons at lines 4 and 8 are between signed int/ptrdiff_t values with no signedness-conversion trap for the analyzed guards.
limitations: A NULL start cannot produce a defined-execution NULL-deref witness: line 4 (`end - start`) is already undefined pointer subtraction before the dereference at line 7; treated as a caller-contract robustness concern, not a confirmed CWE-476.

For nal_length_size >= 5 admitted by a large buffer, res wraps mod 2^32 and may pass line 8, returning a wrong but in-bounds NAL start; no memory-safety or consumer impact is visible, so it is demoted.
res == end - start returns the one-past-end pointer at line 10 (line 8 uses `>`, not `>=`); no consumer of the returned pointer is shown, so no OOB access via that path is confirmable.
If the real caller were shown to derive nal_length_size in 1..4, the negative case would be unreachable; per the fragment-only rule that unshown caller invariant is not used to demote the finding.

verdict.summary: The int parameter `size` is written to zlib's unsigned `avail_in` at line 9 with no validation; a negative value such as -1 is converted to 0xFFFFFFFF and consumed by `inflate` at line 12 as a read length, causing an out-of-bounds read from `src` (signed-to-unsigned conversion into a huge size).

evidence.reason: size is an int parameter whose full declared domain (including negatives) is admitted because no shown statement constrains it; the only checks (deflateInit at line 13, inflateReset at line 21) bound nothing about size. An admitted member, size = -1, is converted by the int->uInt store into 0xFFFFFFFF in z_stream.avail_in, and inflate at line 12 reads up to that many bytes from next_in = src (line 8), with no capacity bound for src visible in the fragment. This is an unvalidated-size flow: signed-to-unsigned conversion of a negative value into a huge size (CWE-195) causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) of the input buffer.

assumptions: z_stream.avail_in is zlib's unsigned 32-bit uInt type, implied by the use of z_stream/inflate/deflate with no other declaration in the fragment.
Line 16's s->block_size*3 - s->zstream.avail_out counts bytes actually written by the first inflate because avail_out only decreases while inflate runs.
No capacity for src, tmpblock, or deflate_block is declared in the fragment; per the missing-bound standard this does not block the size-flow finding for src.
limitations: Integer overflow of s->block_size * 3 (lines 11, 16, 28) or an out-of-range s->deflate_block_size (lines 18, 26) could corrupt avail_out/avail_in and overflow tmpblock/deflate_block, but block_size's and deflate_block_size's types, magnitudes, and provenance are not visible in the fragment, so no overflow witness can be constructed from shown statements.

The return values of the first inflate (line 12), deflate (line 19), and deflateEnd (line 20) are discarded; on failure the derived byte counts remain bounded by the avail_out caps and no security-relevant operation runs on a failure state in the shown code, so this is a robustness concern, not a confirmed flaw.
Reading zs.avail_out after deflateEnd (line 20 vs line 26) is defined behavior because deflateEnd does not modify zs output fields.
NULL src or s dereference is not reachable on any path derivable from the shown code (no NULL-producing statement exists), so it is noted as robustness only.

The concrete overread byte count depends on the unshown capacity of the storage behind src; the finding is confirmed as an unvalidated-size flow by the shown arithmetic alone, hence confidence capped below 0.65.

verdict.summary: In the post-auth D-Bus header path, the value returned by g_dbus_message_bytes_needed (line 73) is forwarded unchecked as the allocation size in buffer_new (line 81). The only guard, `required < 0` (line 74), rejects only negative values and admits every non-negative size; no upper bound on the total message size exists anywhere in the fragment. Because the header bytes (including the body-length field) are attacker-controlled socket data read at line 20, a valid header can drive a multi-GiB allocation, causing host memory exhaustion or a GLib OOM abort in the shared proxy — an attacker-directed, repeatable denial of service (confirmed missing-bound / uncontrolled-allocation flow, CWE-770).

evidence.reason: `required` is an entry-point-derived size: attacker socket bytes are stored into buffer->data by buffer_read (line 20) and parsed by g_dbus_message_bytes_needed (line 73), which derives the full message length from the header contents. The only shown constraint is `if (required < 0)` (line 74), whose admitted set is every non-negative value; no capacity or upper bound on required exists in the fragment, so its residual range is unbounded above. At line 81, buffer_new consumes required as the new buffer's allocation size, so any admitted large value (e.g., a header with a large 32-bit body-length field) forces a very large allocation or an OOM abort (g_malloc) — uncontrolled resource allocation (CWE-770), attacker-directed and repeatable per connection.

assumptions: buffer_read (line 20) is a helper that stores the number of bytes received into buffer->pos with pos <= buffer->size; this bounds the auth-path buffer contents used by lines 34-54.

find_auth_end (line 43) returns -1 when no NUL is present, otherwise the index of the first NUL in [0, buffer->pos), so auth_end is in [1, pos] and extra_data = pos - auth_end (line 49) cannot underflow.
The standard SASL exchange completes (found_auth_end set at line 47, client->authenticated set at lines 60-61), making the post-auth message path at lines 68-90 reachable for normal clients.

g_dbus_message_bytes_needed (line 73) returns -1 on a malformed header and otherwise a non-negative total message length derived from the header, per its standard GLib semantics; the shown `required < 0` check (line 74) relies on exactly this contract.
limitations: An OOB span in g_bytes_new (line 54) via extra_data is not confirmed: with auth_end in [1, pos], extra_data = pos - auth_end is in [0, pos-1] and data[auth_end, auth_end+extra_data) stays within the bytes read at line 20.
No capacity-based OOB claim is made against the g_dbus_message_bytes_needed read at line 73 because the header_buffer capacity (side->header_buffer.size) is not set anywhere in the fragment.

A client that sends a header claiming a large body and then stalls the connection would leave buffer_read (line 20) blocked; this is folded into the same resource-exhaustion concern rather than reported separately.
A possible busy-retry loop if buffer_read (line 20) returned FALSE without closing the side is not confirmed because buffer_read's EOF/error semantics are not shown.
The one-shot overwrite of side->extra_input_data (line 54) and the GError leak on the error path (lines 73-78) are single-shot, non-compounding, and not reported.
On 32-bit builds, a wrap of gssize required could additionally occur; this platform-specific case is subsumed by the same DoS finding and is not reported separately.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write: guest-controlled capset_version (and capset_id) flow unvalidated into virgl_renderer_fill_caps, which writes a version/id-selected payload into resp->capset_data whose capacity is only max_size bytes (line 14). The sole guard (line 10) rejects only max_size==0 and does not constrain the version; max_ver, the natural bound, is computed at lines 8-9 and never used.

evidence.reason: Write sink: the heap region at resp->capset_data has capacity max_size bytes (allocation at line 14 is sizeof(*resp)+max_size, minus the fixed header). gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version are entry-point guest inputs (filled at line 7 via VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD) whose residual ranges are the full uint32 domain [0, 2^32-1] because no shown statement validates them. The only guard on the path, line 10 'if (!max_size)', admits all max_size in [1, 2^32-1] and excludes only 0; it does not test the version and cannot bound the callee's write extent. verdict.summary: hash_passwords substitutes a deterministic all-zero salt for a random per-user salt: line 31 executes std::memset(hashed_passwords[i].salt, 0, 32) on every iteration and the intended RAND_bytes call is commented out (lines 27-30). Because the residual value of the salt is a single constant for all count users and all runs, identical passwords (input origin: argv via line 59, unconstrained) produce identical stored (salt, hash) pairs, defeating per-user salting and enabling precomputed/dictionary and cross-user attacks on the credential database. Confirmed mechanism: predictable zero-entropy salt in a KDF, primary CWE-338.

The next loop iteration then passes start = string_lim + 1 to onig_search (lines 64-65) while end/range are string_lim, an out-of-domain start pointer into the subject buffer that can cause a heap out-of-bounds read inside the regex engine. If onig_search internally validates start > end and returns a mismatch without dereferencing, the overshoot degrades to a wasted call rather than a memory error; the OOB read therefore executes inside the unshown callee, which is why confidence is capped below the demonstrated-witness range.

verdict.summary: This fragment is the fixed form of flashsv2_prime: the only input that reaches a security-relevant dereference on an unguarded path is src, and the guard `if (!src) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;` (lines 5-6) executes before every use of src (lines 10, 14) on every path, admitting only non-NULL src and excluding NULL. No confirmed vulnerability exists; the remaining concerns (negative size feeding zlib avail_in, block_size*3 arithmetic, unchecked inflate/deflate return values) cannot be confirmed as findings because the relevant field types, buffer capacities, and failure-state consumers are not declared in the fragment.

assumptions: zlib's inflate/deflate honor avail_in/avail_out as hard read/write bounds (standard library semantics), so the fragment's derived lengths bound the library accesses.

The differences at line 18 (s->block_size * 3 - s->zstream.avail_out) and line 28 (s->deflate_block_size - zs.avail_out) equal the bytes actually emitted by the preceding inflate/deflate and therefore lie in [0, s->block_size*3] and [0, s->deflate_block_size] respectively.

The declared capacities of s->tmpblock and s->deflate_block are assumed to be consistent with the s->block_size*3 and s->deflate_block_size bounds the fragment itself sets, and are not visible in the fragment.
limitations: size (int, unconstrained in the fragment) is assigned to s->zstream.avail_in at line 11; a negative value would wrap if avail_in is the zlib unsigned uInt, but that type is not declared in the fragment and no backing capacity for src is visible, so the signed-to-unsigned over-read is not confirmable under the fragment-only discipline.

s->block_size * 3 and s->deflate_block_size - zs.avail_out reach inflate/deflate (lines 13-14, 18-21, 28-31), but the types of s->block_size/s->deflate_block_size and the capacities of s->tmpblock/s->deflate_block are not declared in the fragment; no shown arithmetic exceeds a shown capacity, so OOB/integer-overflow claims are unconfirmable.

The return values of inflate (lines 14, 31), deflate (line 21), and deflateEnd (line 22) are discarded; no security-relevant operation in the fragment demonstrably runs on the corresponding failure states, so this is treated as a robustness concern rather than a confirmed error-handling flaw.
Nothing else in the fragment parses or transforms untrusted content (no format-string, command, SQL, path, or log-injection sink with attacker-controlled data).

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in the evidence index guard at line 7: `idx <= area->evidence().size()` admits `idx == size`, so `area->deleteEvidence(idx)` at line 8 runs with an out-of-range index (valid indices are 0..size-1), causing an out-of-bounds access on the evidence container. For an N-element evidence list, N = area->evidence().size() at line 7, valid indices are 0..N-1, but the guard `idx <= N` admits idx == N, which reaches the sink at line 8 as an out-of-range index (excess of exactly 1 past the last valid index). The `<=` should be `<`; the failure is an out-of-bounds access in the mutating call, primary CWE-787, with the incorrect comparison being the root cause.

assumptions: area->evidence().size() at line 7 returns the element count of the same container that area->deleteEvidence(idx) indexes at line 8, so valid indices are 0..size-1.
QString::toInt sets is_int=false for non-numeric or overflowing strings, so after line 7 the admitted idx values are ordinary ints in [0, size].
limitations: argv[0] at line 6 is read with no argv.isEmpty()/argc >= 1 check, which could assert/abort on an empty argument list; this degenerate empty-list precondition is not derived by any shown statement, so it is demoted rather than reported.
`area` is dereferenced (lines 3, 7, 8) with no NULL check shown; a NULL value is not derived by the shown code and depends on unshown caller/framework invariants, so it is demoted.
`argc` and `packet` are unused in the shown fragment.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset forwards the guest-controlled capset_version (filled by VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD at line 7) to virgl_renderer_fill_caps at line 17 with no validation: the only guard, `if (!max_size)` at line 10, constrains the response size but not the version, and the per-capset version ceiling max_ver fetched at line 8 is never applied. Any 32-bit version value (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF) passes the guard for any registered capset and is consumed by the host-side capability-fill routine as its per-version selector, enabling an out-of-bounds access in QEMU's host process (host-memory disclosure and/or crash). The primary defect is the missing bound on an entry-point selector/index argument (CWE-125); the matching allocation `g_malloc(sizeof(*resp) + max_size)` at line 14 is internally consistent with the fill size max_size, so the OOB is in reading the versioned capability table, not in the fragment's own write.

evidence.reason: The sink consumes the entry-point input gc.capset_version (filled from the guest command by VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD at line 7; full uint32 residual range [0, 2^32-1] with no shown constraint). The only guard on the path, `if (!max_size)` at line 10, admits every version for any capset with nonzero max_size, and the version ceiling max_ver returned by virgl_renderer_get_cap_set at line 8 is never compared against gc.capset_version. A witness (capset_id of any registered set with max_size=4096, capset_version=0xFFFFFFFF) passes line 10 and reaches line 17, forwarding an out-of-domain version into the capability-fill routine whose per-version table index the fragment itself bounds (max_ver) but does not enforce — a missing-bound/unvalidated-selector flow causing out-of-bounds reads of per-version capability data in the QEMU host process (CWE-125), with host-memory disclosure/binaries and DoS impact.

assumptions: gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version are 32-bit unsigned integers taken from the guest command payload via VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD (line 7) and consumed by uint32_t-typed library parameters (lines 8-9, 16-17).

virgl_renderer_fill_caps writes max_size bytes into resp->capset_data, the same max_size returned by the paired virgl_renderer_get_cap_set, so the g_malloc(sizeof(*resp) + max_size) allocation at line 14 is size-consistent with the fill on a 64-bit host.
A registered capset has nonzero max_size, which is the value the guard at line 10 admits.
limitations: Uninitialized-response info leak candidate: g_malloc at line 14 leaves heap uninitialized, line 15 sets only resp->hdr.type, and line 19 transmits sizeof(*resp) + max_size bytes; whether copied-but-uninitialized bytes exist depends on the layout of struct virtio_gpu_resp_capset / virtio_gpu_ctrl_hdr, which is not shown in the fragment, so no CWE is attached.

The exact out-of-bounds consequence inside virgl_renderer_fill_caps (read vs write) is not shown; the call-site finding assumes standard per-version capability-table semantics, hence the capped confidence and CWE-125 (read) primary rather than CWE-787.

Unvalidated gc.capset_id into virgl_renderer_get_cap_set/fill_caps: whether the library returns max_size=0 for unknown IDs (absorbed by the line 10 guard) or indexes OOB is an unshown invariant in both directions.

A 32-bit wrap of sizeof(*resp) + max_size at line 14 would require an unshown 32-bit host and a max_size near 2^32, which is not attacker-scaled by this body since max_size is a fixed per-set library value.
g_malloc aborting on OOM (glib contract) for a fixed per-set max_size is a robustness concern, not an attacker-directed finding.

verdict.summary: Command-line option parsing writes unbounded option strings into 10-byte stack buffers via sscanf("%s"), allowing attacker-controlled stack buffer overflows from argv-derived optarg.

evidence.reason: optarg (argv-derived, entry-point) has an unconstrained residual range: the only pre-sink guard, `if (optarg)` at line 92, excludes only NULL and no length cap exists. dr is declared `char dr[10]` at line 94; sscanf's "%s" conversion writes the full token plus a NUL terminator, so an optarg token of length >= 10 writes 11+ bytes into the 10-byte buffer. Witness: -s 1234567890 passes the line 92 guard and overflows by 1 byte at this sink (line 95), with unbounded excess for longer tokens. Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121).

Same mechanism as the -s case: dr is `char dr[10]` at line 105, guarded only by `if (optarg)` at line 103, and sscanf's unbounded "%s" writes token+NUL from the unconstrained argv-derived optarg. An optarg token of length >= 10 overflows the 10-byte buffer at this sink (line 106); the later `format` range check at line 111 runs after the overflow and does not protect it. CWE-121.

Same mechanism as the -s case: dr is `char dr[10]` at line 119, guarded only by `if (optarg)` at line 117, with no width limit on the sscanf "%s" conversion. Any argv-derived optarg token of length >= 10 writes 11+ bytes into the 10-byte buffer at this sink (line 120); the `outputFormat` range check at line 125 runs afterward and cannot prevent the overflow. CWE-121.

Same mechanism as the -s case: dr is `char dr[10]` at line 133, guarded only by `if (optarg)` at line 131, and the sscanf "%s" conversion writes an unbounded token plus NUL from the unconstrained argv-derived optarg. An optarg token of length >= 10 overflows the 10-byte buffer at this sink (line 134); the `object_type` validation at lines 139-142 runs after the overflow. CWE-121.

assumptions: dr is a 10-byte stack array as declared at lines 94, 105, 119, 133.
argv[optind] is valid because line 193 (`(argc - optind) < 1`) returns before its use at lines 208/214.
format is restricted to 1..2 for the file_ext[format] uses at lines 227/240 by line 111 plus the line 193 early return.
limitations: The fread return at line 263 is discarded and header[4..7] may be uninitialized when the input file is shorter than 8 bytes, read at line 268; this only influences the mp4file classification with no security-relevant downstream consumer shown, so it is not reported as a finding.

def_srate (line 289) is passed to decodeAACfile without shown validation, but the callee's contract is not visible and it is not an index/size/length/capacity argument by name or use, so no in-domain failure is confirmable.
Repeated -o/-a options leak prior audioFileName/adtsFileName allocations; bounded by argc and non-compounding, not reported.
file_ext array capacity is not shown; the format 1..2 validation plus early return prevents any derivable out-of-bounds index.

verdict.summary: extract_tar_to_path is vulnerable to symlink-following writes outside the destination. The only path guard, is_path_safe (lines 171-189), rejects only absolute paths and '..' components, and the disk writer is created with options limited to ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM (line 103) without ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS. A tar containing a symlink entry 'l' -> '/tmp/x' followed by a file entry 'l/pwn' passes the first-pass check (line 116) and, in the second pass, lines 144/157 resolve and write through the symlink, creating /tmp/x/pwn outside dest_path (arbitrary file write, CWE-59).

evidence.reason: current_file (line 138) is an unconstrained entry-point field from archive_entry_pathname; it flows through lines 140 and 142 into this filesystem-write sink. The only guard on the path, is_path_safe at line 116, admits any non-absolute path without a '..' component, including symlink names and descendants such as 'l' and 'l/pwn'. The disk-writer options at line 103 contain no ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS, so an earlier symlink entry is followed and this write lands outside dest_path, e.g. /tmp/x/pwn. Primary mechanism: improper link resolution before file access (CWE-59).

Same unconstrained path from line 138 reaches the data write for entries whose header was accepted at line 144. With no ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS option (line 103) and no symlink check in either pass, file content is written through the previously extracted symlink to a location outside dest_path, completing the arbitrary-write impact of the CWE-59 finding.

assumptions: archive_write_disk, configured without ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS/ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT, resolves symlink components in entry paths when writing (documented libarchive default behavior); the fragment's explicit option set at line 103 is TIME | PERM only.
Tar entry pathnames returned by archive_entry_pathname are NUL-terminated strings of unconstrained length; the fragment imposes no length cap on them.
limitations: TOCTOU: the path-safety check (lines 114-122) and the extraction (lines 137-163) are separated by archive_read_free (125) and a fresh archive_read_open_filename (130), and the second pass performs no per-entry is_path_safe check. A concurrently replaced tar_path could extract unvalidated paths, but the fragment does not establish attacker ability to replace that file, and the CWE-59 finding already covers a stable malicious archive.

Unchecked strdup at line 176: on allocation failure strtok dereferences NULL at line 177; allocation size scales with the attacker-controlled path length, but this is only a DoS, not a security-critical operation on the failure state.

archive_entry_pathname could return NULL for a nameless entry and be dereferenced at line 172 without a check; NULL production depends on libarchive internals not visible in the fragment, so no CWE is confirmed.

Statuses of archive_read_data_skip (line 121) and the exit status of the inner read loop (line 156) are discarded; a partial data-read failure can still yield success at line 168 (incomplete extraction), which is a robustness concern, not an attacker-exercised security failure.

snprintf at line 140 truncates entry names longer than 511 bytes; truncated names could collide and overwrite sibling files under dest_path. No traversal and no security-relevant boundary is confirmed.
An empty entry pathname is admitted by is_path_safe and would apply the entry's attributes to dest_path itself; low impact, not a CWE-level finding.

verdict.summary: pktRemoveEvidence reads argv[0] at line 6 without any check that the packet argument list is non-empty; the supplied argc is never used and no argv.size()/isEmpty() guard exists. A packet with zero arguments leaves argv at its full declared domain including the empty list, so argv[0] is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) reachable before the line-7 guard, which only protects the later deleteEvidence(idx) call.

evidence.reason: argv is an entry-point QStringList (packet argument list) whose full declared domain includes the empty list; no shown statement before line 6 constrains its size — argc (line 1) is never tested and no argv.isEmpty()/argv.size() check appears anywhere in the fragment — so its residual range still contains argv == {}. The subscript argv[0] at line 6 then reads element 0 of a size-0 container: an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) that executes before the line-7 guard, which only bounds the later area->deleteEvidence(idx) call at line 8 and therefore cannot protect line 6. Witness: a packet with zero arguments produces argv == {} and argc == 0; line 3 admits the path (checkEvidenceAccess returns true); line 6 performs the unchecked element read before toInt is invoked. The dead argc parameter is the visible missing check.

assumptions: area->evidence().size() at line 7 is the capacity bound for the deleteEvidence(idx) index at line 8; the guard int idx < size() && idx >= 0 admits exactly 0..size()-1 and fully protects that call.
QStringList::operator[] with an index outside [0, size()) is an out-of-bounds access (standard container semantics assumed for the empty-list case).
limitations: The empty-argv witness is a degenerate zero-length input whose minimum is not established by any shown derivation; per calibration rules this caps confidence at 0.65, and any caller-side guarantee that argv is non-empty would be outside the fragment and cannot be used either way.
Exact manifestation of the line-6 OOB read (crash vs. garbage read) depends on Qt internals not shown; the missing-bound mechanism itself is confirmed by the shown statements.
A NULL-area dereference is not reported: the first dereference of area occurs inside the unshown checkEvidenceAccess(area), and no shown statement produces NULL for area.

verdict.summary: Divide-by-zero (FPE, DoS). The AVStream field st->time_base.num (int) is read into the av_rescale denominator with no validation in the shown code; for the admitted input class {time_base.num == 0} the unconditional rescale at L11 computes denominator AV_TIME_BASE * (int64_t)0 = 0 and divides by zero, crashing the process on crafted demuxer input. The same unvalidated field reaches L7/L9 and L15, where the `if (den && num)` guard at L14 constrains only compute_frame_duration outputs, not time_base.num. Additionally av_frac_add at L46/L50 consumes st->pts, whose den member is never assigned or validated in the fragment (zero den in the admitted domain). Negative frame_size and zero den/num from compute_frame_duration are properly excluded by L45 and L14 respectively.

evidence.reason: Sink: unconditional av_rescale whose third argument is the denominator. st->time_base.num (int) is a demuxer-derived struct field with no constraining statement in the fragment, so its residual range is the full int domain including 0. Witness: pkt->duration=0, st->time_base.den=1, st->time_base.num=0 (all members of their declared domains; no guard precedes L11) yields denominator AV_TIME_BASE * (int64_t)0 = 0 and av_rescale divides by zero -> FPE/process crash (CWE-369). The defect is the missing bound/validation on st->time_base.num before it is consumed as a division denominator; no capacity or guard in the shown code neutralizes it.

Sink: av_rescale with denominator den * (int64_t)st->time_base.num. Guards L12 (pkt->duration == 0) and L14 (den && num) execute before the sink and admit the witness {duration=0, num=1, den=1}, but L14 constrains only the compute_frame_duration outputs; st->time_base.num retains its full int residual range. With st->time_base.num == 0 the denominator is 1 * 0 = 0 -> divide-by-zero (FPE) despite the guard, so the L14 protective statement is insufficient for this input class (CWE-369).

Sink: av_frac_add consumes the AVFrac st->pts whose den member is never assigned or validated anywhere in the fragment (residual range = full int including 0). Audio path: witness {codec_type=CODEC_TYPE_AUDIO, frame_size=0, pkt->size=1, st->pts.den=0} passes the L45 guard (frame_size >= 0 admitted; pkt->size non-zero) and the switch case at L41-L42, reaching L46 with a zero denominator inside av_frac_add -> FPE/unbounded normalization (CWE-369).

Sink: av_frac_add in the video case, executed unconditionally when st->codec.codec_type == CODEC_TYPE_VIDEO. st->pts.den is unvalidated (full int residual range including 0), so a zero denominator reaches av_frac_add -> FPE/unbounded normalization (CWE-369). No statement in the shown code constrains st->pts.den before this call.

assumptions: AV_TIME_BASE is the standard nonzero compile-time constant (1000000), so the zero value of the rescale denominator at L7/L9/L11 is produced solely by st->time_base.num == 0.
av_rescale(a, b, c) performs a division by its third argument c; a zero c is out of the operation's domain (standard arithmetic semantics, callee body not shown).
st->pts is an AVFrac/AVRational-like accumulator whose den member (int) is the normalizing denominator consumed by av_frac_add.
CODEC_TYPE_AUDIO and CODEC_TYPE_VIDEO are distinct constants selectable via st->codec.codec_type; pkt/st struct fields have the int/int64 declared types used in the analysis.
The fragment is reached during demuxer packet processing, so st/pkt fields are entry-point-derived data; per the rules their residual ranges start from their full declared domains.
limitations: NULL-dereference of the st/pkt parameters themselves (L2, L6+) is demoted: no shown path produces NULL and no container/lookup derives these pointers inside the fragment.

int64 overflow of the a*b product inside av_rescale (e.g., pts near INT64_MAX with large time_base.den) is demoted: the corrupted timestamp feeds only timing metadata and comparisons (L19-L36, L38-L39), not an allocation/index/length/format sink, so the CWE-190 security-consumer standard is not met.
Unary negation of pkt->duration at L27 demoted: requires duration == INT64_MIN whose production is not shown, and the result is timing metadata only.
Negative frame_size from get_audio_frame_size is fully protected by the L45 guard (frame_size >= 0 excludes all negative ints before the L46 sink).

Zero den/num produced by compute_frame_duration are fully excluded by the L14 guard (den && num) for that specific zero-source class; L15 remains vulnerable only via the separate time_base.num == 0 class.

The fragment contains no loops; internal loops in unshown callees (compute_frame_duration, av_frac_add, get_audio_frame_size) are out of scope; get_audio_frame_size's internal behavior is unknown and only its return sign is relied on.
The primary witness is a range claim (any stream with time_base.num == 0), not a single exact demonstrated magnitude, which accounts for the 0.62 confidence rather than a higher value.

verdict.summary: evaluate_utility_inc uses elbg->numCB as a loop bound with no visible capacity check: for i in [0, numCB-1] it reads elbg->utility[i] and writes elbg->utility_inc[i] (lines 5-7). numCB is unconstrained above the body-executing minimum of 1, and neither array has any declared capacity in the fragment, so any numCB exceeding the arrays' (unshown) allocation drives an out-of-bounds read and write. The missing bound on this input-derived size/index is the defect; the line-5 comparison guards only the accumulation at line 6 and does not protect the accesses.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): the write index i is the loop counter running [0, elbg->numCB-1] per line 4's predicate 'i < elbg->numCB'. elbg->numCB has residual range [1, INT_MAX] with no upper bound imposed by any shown statement, and elbg->utility_inc has no declared capacity anywhere in the fragment, so the number of elements written (numCB) is an out-of-domain count with no visible bound — the missing-bound (unvalidated-size flow) is confirmed by the shown arithmetic alone. An admitted numCB greater than the actual utility_inc allocation writes out of bounds on every iteration at or after index = allocation size.

Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the same unconstrained elbg->numCB (residual [1, INT_MAX]) drives index i over [0, numCB-1] into elbg->utility, whose capacity is never declared in the fragment (bytes 5-6 repeat the read at line 6). With no visible bound tying numCB to the utility allocation, an admitted numCB exceeding that allocation reads out of bounds at index = allocation size. The line-5 comparison only gates the accumulation at line 6; it does not bound i or numCB, and the read happens before the comparison can affect anything.

assumptions: elbg->numCB is an integer: it must satisfy 'i < elbg->numCB' for i=0 for the loop body to run, so on the body-executing path numCB >= 1 (line 4).
elbg->utility and elbg->utility_inc are integer arrays whose element capacities are not declared or derived anywhere in the fragment; their relationship to numCB is unshown.
limitations: NULL dereference of elbg (line 4) and the member pointers is not reported: no shown statement produces NULL, and for this static internal helper the object is caller-constructed, making it a caller-contract robustness concern rather than a demonstrated finding.

Signed integer overflow in 'elbg->numCB*elbg->utility[i]' (line 5) and 'inc += elbg->utility[i]' (line 6) is not reported: the types of numCB, utility[i], and error are not declared in the fragment, so a wrap cannot be confirmed in the shown types, and the corrupted value is only stored into utility_inc with no in-fragment security-relevant consumer (index/size/length/pointer) of the stored value.

The OOB claim is a range claim (numCB greater than the unshown allocation), not a single-value witness, because the capacity of utility/utility_inc is not visible; confidence is capped accordingly at 0.55.

verdict.summary: Command injection in controller::bookmark: feed-controlled title, description, and feed_title are embedded as unquoted %s slots into cmdline (line 10) and executed via /bin/sh -c (lines 27-31) or run_interactively (line 22) with no visible shell-metacharacter validation or escaping for those fields. A title such as "x;id;#" executes arbitrary commands. Only the URL slot is protected (single-quote removal at line 12 plus quoting), leaving the other three inputs unconstrained.

evidence.reason: Sink: cmdline, carrying title/description/feed_title with their full std::string residual domain (no shown constraint anywhere; lines 13-15 pass them through unshown stfl::quote/quote_empty helpers, which cannot establish a shell-escaping bound), is executed as `/bin/sh -c` (my_argv[2] at line 29). The line-9 guard (bookmark_cmd.length() > 0) is admitted for any configured command, and the line-19 branch only selects the execution path. Witness title = "x;id;#" yields cmdline = "bookmark.sh 'https://example.com/a' x;id;# ...", where sh executes `bookmark.sh ... x`, then `id` after the `;`. The mechanism is arbitrary command execution via unvalidated shell metacharacters (CWE-78).

Distinct execution sink on the interactive branch: the same cmdline built at line 10 from the unconstrained title/description/feed_title inputs is run interactively. No validation separates the taint origin (lines 13-15) from this sink; the same witness (title = "x;id;#") reaches shell interpretation here when line 19's guard admits is_interactive. Primary mechanism: command injection (CWE-78).

assumptions: bookmark_cmd and is_interactive (lines 7-8) originate from the local trusted configuration, so the unquoted first %s slot for bookmark_cmd is by design and not attacker-controlled.
Execution on the non-interactive path uses /bin/sh -c (lines 27-31), i.e., POSIX shell semantics in which a single-quoted segment is literal except for a single quote.
cfg.get_configvalue/get_configvalue_as_bool return valid values; no NULL or failed-lookup state is possible on the shown path.
limitations: The URL slot is not reported as a finding: line 12 replaces every ' with %27 and line 10 places the result in a single-quoted slot, so no character that can terminate the POSIX single-quoted segment reaches the shell.
Log injection (CWE-117) via CR/LF in title/description/feed_title reaching the LOG write at line 17 is plausible but only logged at DEBUG and shares the same taint; not carried as a separate CWE.

The bodies of stfl::quote and quote_empty are not shown; if they performed shell escaping they would neutralize this injection, but no such bound is derivable from the fragment, and per the analysis rules an unshown helper cannot establish safety.
Discarded return values of v->push_empty_formaction/stfl::reset/v->pop_current_formaction and utils::run_interactively are UI-flow concerns with no security-relevant consumer here.
const_cast on string literals at lines 27-29 is benign because the pointed-to literals are never modified.

verdict.summary: pkt->duration (int64_t) reaches security-relevant sinks with no visible bound: line 11 rescales it unconditionally (no AV_NOPTS_VALUE/positivity check, unlike pts/dts), and line 27 negates it at st->last_IP_pts= -pkt->duration. For the admitted value INT64_MIN (AV_NOPTS_VALUE), the negation is signed-integer overflow (UB) and the corrupted duration feeds pkt->dts/st->cur_dts and the timestamp comparisons that gate mux success, causing undefined behavior and spurious rejection/corrupted stream state. A local bound such as 'if (pkt->duration > 0)' is absent on the shown path.

evidence.reason: CWE-190 primary sink: pkt->duration is an internal-helper int64_t parameter with residual range INT64_MIN..INT64_MAX (no shown statement bounds it; line 11's rescale has no visible output constraint, and lines 12-26 leave the value untouched on the admitting path). Path: pts=0 (line 6 admits), dts=AV_NOPTS_VALUE (line 8 skips), duration=AV_NOPTS_VALUE (INT64_MIN), b_frames=1 (line 25 admits), last_IP_pts=AV_NOPTS_VALUE (line 26 admits). Negating INT64_MIN overflows int64 (UB); the wrapped value is stored into last_IP_pts/pkt->dts (lines 30, 46-47) and consumed by the timestamp comparisons at lines 42/38 that gate mux success, so the corruption is not inconsequential. The base64 branch does not NUL-terminate buffer (no +1 margin), but no shown consumer requires NUL termination since later reads are length-bounded via the length argument (line 26); not independently confirmed.

verdict.summary: Multiple unbounded stack copies of command-line input into fixed-size buffers: strcpy(aacFileName, argv[optind]) (line 196), strcpy(audioFileName, optarg) (line 69), strcpy(adtsFileName, optarg) (line 76), and four sscanf(optarg, "%s", dr) calls writing into a 10-byte local (lines 83, 94, 108, 122). The only guards are non-NULL checks (lines 66/73/80/91/105/119) and an argument-existence check (line 181); none bounds input length, so a 300-byte option argument or filename overflows the visible 255-byte arrays (lines 19–21) or dr[10] (lines 82/93/107/121), yielding a stack buffer overflow (CWE-121).

evidence.reason: argv[optind] is entry-point command-line input whose residual length is unbounded: the only guard on the path, line 181 `if (((argc - optind) < 1) || showHelp)`, guarantees the argument exists but never caps its size. strcpy writes strlen+1 bytes; the destination `char aacFileName[255];` (line 19) holds only 255 bytes, so a 300-character filename writes 301 bytes and overflows the stack buffer (CWE-121).

optarg for -o is entry-point input with no length constraint: the guard `if (optarg)` (line 66) excludes only NULL. An argument of 300 bytes is admitted and strcpy writes 301 bytes into `char audioFileName[255];` (line 20), overflowing the stack buffer (CWE-121).

optarg for -a is entry-point input constrained only by `if (optarg)` (line 73), which excludes NULL but not long strings. A 300-byte argument writes 301 bytes into `char adtsFileName[255];` (line 21), overflowing the stack buffer (CWE-121).

optarg for -s is entry-point input; %s writes the full whitespace-delimited token plus NUL into `char dr[10];` (line 82) with no width specifier. A 10-character token (e.g., 1234567890) is admitted by `if (optarg)` (line 80) and by the match-count test, writing 11 bytes into the 10-byte stack buffer (CWE-121).

optarg for -f is entry-point input; %s into `char dr[10];` (line 93) has no width limit. A 10+ character token is admitted by `if (optarg)` (line 91) and overflows dr by writing token+NUL (11 bytes for a 10-char token), before the format-range check at lines 99–100 can set showHelp (CWE-121).

optarg for -b is entry-point input; %s into `char dr[10];` (line 107) is unbounded. A 10+ character token is admitted by `if (optarg)` (line 105) and writes token+NUL (11+ bytes) into the 10-byte buffer, overflowing the stack before the outputFormat check at lines 113–114 (CWE-121).

optarg for -l is entry-point input; %s into `char dr[10];` (line 121) has no width bound. A 10+ character token is admitted by `if (optarg)` (line 119) and overflows dr (token + NUL), executing before the object_type validation at lines 127–133 and before the showHelp return at lines 181–185 (CWE-121).

assumptions: Capacities quoted from declarations: aacFileName[255] (line 19), audioFileName[255] (line 20), adtsFileName[255] (line 21), header[8] (line 22), dr[10] (lines 82, 93, 107, 121).
Guard at line 181 ensures argv[optind] exists (non-NULL) but is read as imposing no length bound.
if (optarg) guards (lines 66, 73, 80, 91, 105, 119) admit all non-NULL strings.
limitations: strcat(audioFileName, file_ext[format]) at line 216 could also overflow, but the extension string lengths in file_ext are not visible in the fragment, so it is not confirmed.

fread return value is discarded at line 239; on reads shorter than 8 bytes, header[4..7] are uninitialized when compared at line 244 and pushed back at lines 254–261 (CWE-457 candidate), but no security-relevant consumer of the uninitialized values is shown in the fragment.
Pushing back 8 bytes via ungetc (lines 254–261) exceeds the C standard's 1-byte pushback guarantee; failure is implementation-defined and not a memory-safety sink in the shown code.

CR/LF injection into stderr via aacFileName at faad_fprintf calls (lines 221, 234, 280) is a possible log-injection (CWE-117) candidate; it was not counted because the data is same-actor command-line input and the impact within the shown code is limited to terminal output formatting.
strcpy(audioFileName, aacFileName) at line 209 is a second writer on the line-196 overflow path, not an independent root cause.

verdict.summary: dprintf_formatf writes attacker-scaled output into the fixed stack buffer work[BUFFSIZE] (line 25): format- or varargs-derived width/precision (lines 336-345, residual range [0, LONG_MAX] after the sign guards at 358/364) are passed unvalidated to libc sprintf at line 384, and the integer/pointer precision path fills leading zeros with an unvalidated count at lines 205-208, both overflowing the buffer.

evidence.reason: width/precision are entry-point inputs (varargs via (long)vto[p->width].data.num.as_signed at lines 339/345, or format-encoded via p->width/p->precision at lines 337/343); the only guards on the path, if(width >= 0) at line 358 and if(prec >= 0) at line 364, admit [0, LONG_MAX] and impose no upper bound relative to work[BUFFSIZE] (declared line 25). An admitted width or precision such as 1000000 makes libc sprintf emit >= 1000000 bytes into the BUFFSIZE-byte stack array, overflowing it by >= 1000000 - BUFFSIZE + 1 bytes (CWE-121, stack-based buffer overflow).

prec is entry-point input with residual range [0, LONG_MAX] (line 119 via FLAGS_PRECPARAM after the sign guard at 122-125, or line 128 via FLAGS_PREC unguarded); after subtracting the <= 22-digit count at line 198, the guard if(prec > 0) at line 205 admits every value >= 1 and the loop at 207-208 writes that many bytes *w-- descending from near &work[sizeof(work)-2] (line 32) with no check against the start of work[BUFFSIZE] (line 25). For example '%.1000000x' writes ~999999 zeros before &work[0], an out-of-bounds write below the stack array (CWE-787).

assumptions: work[BUFFSIZE] (line 25) has the compile-time capacity BUFFSIZE; the macro's exact value is not shown, so overflow magnitudes are expressed relative to it.
FLAGS_WIDTHPARAM/FLAGS_PRECPARAM/FLAGS_WIDTH/FLAGS_PREC are set by dprintf_Pass1 for '*'- and 'N'-style width/precision specifiers, as implied by the branches at lines 102, 118, 127, 336, and 342.
vto[].data.num.as_signed is a 64-bit signed type (mp_intmax_t); the casts to long at lines 103/119/339/345 preserve the value range.
limitations: The positional-parameter index p = &vto[param] at line 99 is unvalidated against MAX_PARAMETERS (line 21), but whether dprintf_DollarString/dprintf_Pass1 can actually produce an out-of-range param depends on their unshown bodies; not claimed as a finding.
The %n-family stores at lines 394-402 write through caller-supplied p->data.ptr with no NULL check; the pointer's validity is a caller contract, not attacker-directed through shown statements.
strlen(str) at line 274 assumes the %s argument is a NUL-terminated C string (caller contract); no shown statement produces an unterminated string.
Huge width values create very large OUTCHAR loops (lines 218-219, 237-238, 282-283, 317-323); OUTCHAR/stream semantics are not shown, so resource exhaustion is not claimed.
formatbuf (line 330) could itself be overrun at lines 360-368 only if curl_msnprintf returned would-be lengths instead of written lengths; its semantics are unshown.
width -= prec at line 206 can wrap for huge magnitudes, but no security-relevant consumer of the wrapped width was demonstrated; not claimed.

verdict.summary: png_zalloc divides PNG_UINT_32_MAX by the unvalidated parameter size at line 14. size is an internal-helper parameter with full uInt domain 0..UINT_MAX and is never constrained by the shown code; on the witness (png_ptr != NULL, items = 1, size = 0) the division PNG_UINT_32_MAX/0 executes on every path through line 14, which is undefined behavior and typically raises SIGFPE, terminating the process (denial of service). The missing protective statement is a size == 0 short-circuit before the division.

evidence.reason: size is declared at line 1 as uInt with the full domain 0..UINT_MAX, and no statement in the fragment constrains it (line 8 only checks png_ptr; line 14 bounds items given size, never size itself). The divisor PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size at line 14 is evaluated on every path that reaches it, before any admission decision of the guard, so the admitted input size = 0 (with png_ptr != NULL per line 8, items = 1) triggers integer division by zero — undefined behavior resulting in a SIGFPE process crash on typical platforms. Primary mechanism: CWE-369 divide by zero, reachable DoS from an unvalidated internal-helper parameter.

assumptions: PNG_UINT_32_MAX is the 32-bit unsigned maximum (2^32 - 1), as implied by its name and use as a png_uint_32 bound in line 14.
uInt is an unsigned integer type whose domain includes 0 and is not narrowed by any visible cast before the division at line 14.
The only guard before line 14 is the png_ptr NULL check at line 8, whose admitted set (non-NULL png_ptr) does not intersect the size domain in any protective way.
Integer division by zero is undefined behavior per the C standard; on mainstream platforms (e.g., x86) it raises SIGFPE and aborts the process.
limitations: The callers of png_zalloc are not shown, so attacker-reachable delivery of size == 0 cannot be demonstrated from the fragment alone; per internal-helper-parameter discipline the full uInt domain is nonetheless the residual range, and the missing validation is the defect.
The multiplication at line 19 was analyzed and is protected by the line 14 guard for every size > 0, so no CWE-190/CWE-787 overflow finding is reported.
The NULL check at line 26 protects the 1.0.X memset path, and the non-1.0.X build returns NULL without dereferencing, so no CWE-476 finding is reported.
The two memsets at lines 31-33 and 37 rewrite exactly num_bytes bytes matching the line 22 allocation, so no CWE-125/787 out-of-bounds finding is reported.
png_size_t and PNG_FLAG_MALLOC_NULL_MEM_OK are not defined in the fragment; no truncation or flag semantics beyond the shown usage were assumed.

verdict.summary: The FORMAT_INT path applies no upper bound to the format-supplied precision: an input like "%.2147483647d" with value 0 drives the loop at lines 207-208 to write prec zeros downward from &work[sizeof(work)-2], overflowing the stack buffer work[BUFFSIZE] (line 25) by an attacker-chosen amount (CWE-787). Independently, the FORMAT_DOUBLE path's caps (lines 359-360, 376-377) still admit prec = sizeof(work)-2 and clamp larger values only to sizeof(work)-3, so (sprintf)(work, formatbuf, dnum) at line 396 emits sizeof(work)+1 or more bytes, overflowing work by 1-2 bytes (CWE-121).

evidence.reason: Sink of the primary CWE-787: 'prec' is entry-point-derived (format precision via p->precision at line 128 or *-parameter at line 119) with residual range [1, LONG_MAX] on the FORMAT_INT path; the only visible guards, 'if(prec == -1) prec = 1;' (lines 188-189) and 'prec -= (long)(workend - w);' (line 198, subtracts at most ~22 digits), impose no upper bound. 'w' starts at '&work[sizeof(work) - 2]' (line 32) and this loop decrements it 'prec' times, writing below work[0] for any prec > sizeof(work); capacity is 'char work[BUFFSIZE]' (line 25). Witness: format "%.2147483647d" with integer argument 0 (num == 0 skips line 193, w stays workend, guard at line 205 admits) yields 2,147,483,647 backward writes, OOB after sizeof(work) iterations. No protective statement bounds this loop; the opaque Pass1 return check (lines 35-36) is not a shown bound.

Independent CWE-121: width/precision derive from the format string (lines 336-345). The caps at lines 359-360 admit width == sizeof(work)-1, and the cap at lines 376-377 admits prec == sizeof(work)-2 unchanged (guard is strict '>'), clamping larger values to sizeof(work)-3. For dnum = -1.0, sprintf emits sign + 1 integer digit + '.' + prec digits = 3 + prec characters; with prec = sizeof(work)-2 that is sizeof(work)+1 chars plus NUL = sizeof(work)+2 bytes into the sizeof(work)-byte buffer declared at line 25; even the clamped value sizeof(work)-3 yields sizeof(work)+1 bytes. The caps under-count by 2 (sign and decimal point), so every admitted large precision overflows; no statement between line 377 and 396 constrains the write.

assumptions: Capacity of 'work' is BUFFSIZE elements, i.e., 'sizeof(work)' (declared line 25); workend is '&work[sizeof(work) - 2]' (line 32), so BUFFSIZE >= 3 is implied and all overflow accounts are exact in terms of sizeof(work) without needing BUFFSIZE's numeric value.
p->precision and p->width hold long values parsed from the attacker-supplied format string; the fragment assigns them to 'long prec'/'long width' at lines 115 and 128 and reads them at 336-345.
num == 0 is a legal integer argument (printf("%.5d", 0) is well-formed).
OUTCHAR writes to the 'stream' callback and imposes no in-fragment length cap.
limitations: vto[param]/endpos indexing (lines 99, 423): 'param' is format-derived (line 89) with no visible bound vs MAX_PARAMETERS (lines 21-22); the only candidate absorber is the opaque 'dprintf_Pass1' call (lines 35-36) whose validation contract is not shown. Under the fragment-only rule neither safety nor confirmation can be fully established, so this index-validation gap is recorded here (same CWE-787 class as the primary) and not added as an extra CWE.

size_t underflow of 'maxprec' for |dnum| >= 10^255 (lines 369-374) makes 'prec = maxprec-1' (line 377) an implementation-defined narrowing; it does not create a new overflow but shows the double-path cap is value-dependent.

Signed overflow on '-LONG_MIN' (line 109) and on '--width'/'width--' with LONG_MIN (lines 140, 218, 236, 246, 282, 288, 317, 322) is UB and can yield unbounded output loops; treated as robustness, not a confirmed memory finding.
Unbounded OUTCHAR output loops for huge widths on the integer path (e.g., line 218) are a resource-exhaustion concern (CWE-770), not counted to keep the verdict focused on memory corruption.
%s with a non-NUL-terminated pointer (lines 274, 285-286) and %n pointer writes (lines 409-417) rely on printf caller contracts not visible in the fragment.

The erroneous 'left' bookkeeping at line 380 (no 'left -= len' after the precision write) does not currently reach an overflow because the precision value fed to '."%ld"' is capped, so formatbuf[32] remains in bounds in the analyzed value ranges.

verdict.summary: The logout handler lets an attacker-controlled hostname-less URL (e.g. protocol-relative "//attacker.example/x") pass the host validation at L39-41, which only errors when uri.hostname is non-NULL, and forwards it at L94 to the redirect handler (open redirect, CWE-601). Independently, the raw logout URL is written to logs before and regardless of the CR/LF check (L9) and is embedded verbatim into the log messages on the validation-failure paths (L30-31, L56-58), enabling log injection (CWE-117).

evidence.reason: Open redirect (CWE-601): url is an entry-point request parameter filled at L7 with no shown sanitization. On the else path, L39-41 raises an error only when (uri.hostname != NULL) AND the two-way strstr test fails, explicitly admitting uri.hostname == NULL; a scheme-less/protocol-relative value such as "//attacker.example/x" (no CR/LF, so L53 is silent) reaches this sink unchanged when provider == NULL (a state the L67 guard explicitly tolerates), and oidc_handle_logout_request redirects the user to it, resolving protocol-relatively to the attacker host. The missing bound is a validation that requires a non-NULL, equal hostname for any URL allowed to reach the redirect sink.

Log injection (CWE-117): url is written to the log before any validation executes (the CR/LF rejection is at L53, which runs later and only on the else path). The entry-point value's full string domain includes literal CR/LF (the L53 check's existence confirms CR/LF-bearing values are in the model), so a value like "...%0d%0aEVIL" reaches this printf-style log sink with no escaping or stripping on the path, forging log records.

Log injection (CWE-117): on the apr_uri_parse failure path, L30 embeds the unvalidated attacker url (which may contain CR/LF; e.g. "http://x/%0d%0aINJECTED") into error_description and this write emits it verbatim; the L53 sanitization later in the function cannot retroactively protect this earlier sink.

Log injection (CWE-117): this sink executes precisely when L53 has admitted a url containing literal "\n" or "\r" (that is the failure set the guard detects); L56 embeds that same url with its CR/LF intact into error_description, and this write logs the CR/LF that the check exists to reject, allowing log-line fabrication.

assumptions: url is an attacker-controlled entry-point input: filled at L7 from the logout request parameter with no visible decoding or validation statement before the sinks.
provider == NULL is an admitted state on the L94 path because the guard at L67 explicitly tests it; no shown statement guarantees a provider.

apr_uri_parse accepts scheme-less/protocol-relative input and leaves uri.hostname NULL (APR documented behavior; not visible in the fragment) — this is the single library-semantics assumption in the CWE-601 chain.
oidc_handle_logout_request redirects the user to the supplied URL (sink semantics implied by its name and by the module's own comment at L52 that URL validation exists to prevent header splitting).
oidc_debug/oidc_error are printf-style log writes that pass their arguments through without sanitization (shown format strings are literals with %s placeholders).
limitations: Trigger semantics of oidc_is_front_channel_logout / oidc_is_back_channel_logout (L11-13) are not shown, so the L12 path passing completely unvalidated url to the redirect sink is noted but not counted as a separately confirmed bypass.
Whether oidc_util_html_send_error escapes error_description (L32/47/59) is unshown, so reflected XSS in the error pages is not confirmed.

With provider != NULL, the hostname-less url is percent-escaped at L89 and the attacker-controlled post_logout_redirect_uri is executed by the IdP one hop beyond the fragment; the confirmed CWE-601 anchor is the provider == NULL direct-redirect path at L94.
NULL return of oidc_get_current_url_host consumed by strstr at L40 is treated as a non-attacker-directed robustness concern, not a finding.

If the apr_uri_parse NULL-hostname assumption were rejected, the open-redirect finding would reduce to the IdP-side execution only; the CWE-117 log-injection finding is independent of that assumption.
